title: Germany Weighs Startup's Low-Cost Cruise Missile to Close Strike Gap as Poland Moves Toward Its Own Starlink
subhead: The German military opened talks with VC-backed US-Israeli startup Covenant over its Anthem cruise missile, a production-ready rival to Taurus and Tomahawk, while Poland inked a letter of intent with ICEYE and PGZ toward a domestic satellite-communications constellation. Both moves point to Europe's accelerating push for independent long-range strike and space capability.

sections.heading: Germany in Talks With Startup Covenant Over Low-Cost Anthem Cruise Missile
sections.body:
Germany's defense ministry confirmed on Friday it is in negotiations with Covenant, a U.S.-Israeli, venture capital-backed startup that emerged from two years of stealth mode this week, over its Anthem cruise missile — a weapon that could quickly close a gaping hole in Berlin's long-range strike arsenal, Defense News reports. The portfolio is shaky on several fronts: a new version of the Taurus air-launched missile is years from fielding, envisioned U.S. Tomahawk deliveries look iffy after heavy use in the American-Israeli war against Iran, and the pan-European ELSA development effort is just starting.

Covenant claims the ground-launched Anthem is production-ready, with flight tests already running weekly, and pitches a mid-six-figure per-unit price — versus $1 million-plus for a current-generation Taurus. Reuters previously reported that target figure. Serial production in Germany is set to begin in Q1 2027 at a Leipzig-area facility, according to a Berlin lobbying firm handling the company's media queries. A third plant is in Israel, and the main facility sits in Grand Prairie, Texas. The company employs roughly 200 people. Its pitch to governments: 'Anthem is built on local production lines so allied governments buy directly from an industrial base they can rely on.'
sections.whyItMatters: A production-ready, low-cost cruise missile from an unproven startup landing German talks shows how the long-range strike gap — exposed by Taurus delays and Tomahawk doubts — is pulling nontraditional vendors into NATO's core strike market, and how fast cost becomes the deciding factor.

sections.heading: Poland Moves Toward a Domestic 'Starlink' With ICEYE-PGZ MilSatCom Deal
sections.body:
Finnish space company ICEYE and Poland's state defense giant PGZ signed a letter of intent to jointly develop a military satellite communications system, with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declaring at the MSPO defense show in Kielce that the project 'can and will be a Polish Starlink.' The program is slated to run from 2026 to 2030, Defense News reports.

ICEYE acts as technology partner, handling satellite system architecture, platform design and manufacturing, and satellite operations, while PGZ organizes the domestic industrial base. The cooperation builds on ICEYE's existing work with PGZ under the MikroSAR synthetic-aperture-radar Earth-observation program, the first component of Warsaw's planned military space toolkit. 'Anyone closely following the Russian-Ukrainian war knows how important communications are,' Tusk said. 'Without communications, you have nothing to look for on the modern battlefield.'
sections.whyItMatters: Poland is deliberately building sovereign military space capability rather than relying on U.S. networks, part of a wider European drive to hedge against dependence on American commercial services like SpaceX's Starlink.

sections.heading: USAF Accelerates Reaper Replacement as Iran War Losses Mount
sections.body:
Heavy combat losses of MQ-9 Reapers are speeding up the U.S. Air Force's push to field a cheaper, more attritable successor, the Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA). Lt. Gen. Christopher J. Niemi, the Air Force's chief modernization officer, said Thursday that the service wants at least 180 MMA airframes at roughly a $10 million price point — about half the bare-airframe cost of the Collaborative Combat Aircraft awarded to Anduril and General Atomics in June — Defense One reports.

The Washington Post reported in August that at least 45 MQ-9s, roughly one-quarter of the fleet, were lost during the war on Iran against a per-unit cost of nearly $82 million in today's dollars. Niemi acknowledged the discussion 'got accelerated' by combat losses. 'You're going to lose more military hardware in future conflicts than you have historically,' he said, 'and that's what's driving us to this fundamental principle that we need things that are easier to produce, cheaper to buy, and that we can afford to lose.' The Army-backed $10 million figure covers the bare airframe only, not missionized sensors, and targets a 2,800-pound payload with a 2,300-nautical-mile radius and 8,000-nautical-mile one-way range per a July DIU solicitation. General Atomics is defending the upgraded MQ-9B SkyGuardian as the path forward, but top service officials are skeptical.
sections.whyItMatters: The attrition economics of the Iran war are reshaping USAF's uncrewed acquisition strategy toward deliberately expendable platforms — a doctrinal shift from exquisite to attritable that will set the template for NATO drone programs.

sections.heading: Iran Likely to Reverse-Engineer Captured Anduril Underwater Drone
sections.body:
Iran's capture of a U.S. military underwater drone — an Anduril Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle — gives Tehran an opportunity to study and potentially reverse-engineer the vessel, Reuters reports. The IRGC says it recovered the drone in the Strait of Hormuz on Sept. 8, posting imagery of it 'fully intact.' U.S. Central Command's Capt. Tim Hawkins called it a defective older model that 'neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,' while Anduril promoted the Dive-LD as 'the most reliable and flexible' large AUV available, capable of operating up to 10 days.

Analysts caution Iran is unlikely to gain a decisive military advantage, but the episode is a propaganda win for Tehran and a setback to Washington's technological-superiority messaging. Iran's embassies in Ghana and Hyderabad publicly mocked the U.S., with one promising an 'unboxing ceremony by our reverse engineers, tomorrow morning.' Bryan Clark of the Hudson Institute noted Iranian engineers 'could definitely reverse-engineer the mechanical systems,' given Tehran's track record with the captured RQ-170 Sentinel stealth drone in 2011. The Dive-LD was also the testbed for Australia's Ghost Shark large underwater drone.
sections.whyItMatters: The loss of a next-generation AUV to a peer adversary, whatever the Pentagon's downplaying, follows a pattern — Iran previously reverse-engineered the RQ-170 — and signals the rising strategic stakes of the underwater-drone race in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

sections.heading: NATO Allies Foil Russian Subsea Cable Sabotage Drill Near Svalbard
sections.body:
NATO allies caught Russian submarines training to deploy destructive technology against undersea cables in Arctic waters near the remote Svalbard archipelago this spring, Reuters reports, citing two Western officials. Moscow's GUGI undersea warfare directorate used deep-sea submersibles to simulate deployment of the technology. A joint operation by Britain, Norway and the United States tracked and confronted the Russian vessels, preventing them from completing the exercise; the ships eventually left the area.

The discovery of the specific weapon, the location, and U.S. involvement were previously unreported, though Britain and Norway disclosed in April that they uncovered a covert Russian operation in Arctic waters. The target cables — two 1,400 km fiber-optic links running up to 2,700 meters deep — carry satellite data from the SvalSat ground station, the world's largest and part of NASA's Near Space Network. Reuters adds that some U.S. intelligence analysts are increasingly concerned Russia may test NATO's Article 5, with cable destruction a potential component; CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow in August in part to warn against escalating sabotage.
sections.whyItMatters: Subsea cable sabotage has moved from theoretical threat to a rehearsed, detectable operation against critical infrastructure — a gray-zone capability with real potential to trigger a NATO response, and the kind of asymmetric target that matters as much as front-line combat.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Asks Washington for Help Against Houthis, Gets Intelligence Only
sections.body:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman sought U.S. military assistance Thursday to fight Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, but Washington declined direct military action, offering intelligence sharing and targeting support instead, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters. Trump held at least two phone calls with the Saudi leader, and U.S. Central Command's Adm. Brad Cooper traveled to Riyadh for talks. A senior administration official said the U.S. is focused on protecting freedom of navigation 'while empowering our regional partners to take the lead.'

The request marks a reversal: back in July, Saudi Arabia insisted it could handle the Houthis alone and urged Washington not to escalate the war. The change comes as Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping and Saudi oil installations rise, and after Iran claiming control of the Strait of Hormuz effectively pushed Saudi reliance onto the Red Sea route — a second corridor the Houthis can squeeze on Iran's behalf. The U.S. official's framing, and the intelligence-only response, suggests Washington does not want a second front in the Gulf while its Iran war drags into its seventh month.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington quietly drawing a line on direct Gulf military engagement — even for a key ally — signals both overstretch in the Iran war and a deliberate push to shift the burden of regional defense onto partners, changing the calculus for Saudi force planning and arms needs.

sections.heading: Anthropic: Russia Uses US-Built AI to Build Autonomous Killer Drones
sections.body:
Anthropic said Thursday that Kremlin-backed actors used its Claude AI to program autonomous lethal drones, improve hacking and influence operations, and avoid detection, Defense One reports. The company's report describes a Russian 'freelance' group, GTG-27005, that used Claude to build an AI model small enough to run on single-board computers yet able to select targets — including a 'person' target class — and 'issue detonation commands without a human in the loop.' The group also used Claude to let autonomous drones communicate with one another for better targeting, and was conducting hardware-in-the-loop testing, though the model had not yet been deployed in the field. Anthropic banned the group and shared findings with industry.

Anthropic also said it detected Chinese and Yemeni groups trying to use Claude to design conventional weapons, plus campaigns using its tools for data theft, malware, and building networks of fake social media profiles and news sites — including forging documents from the Central African Republic Gendarmerie and Ministry of Defense. The report follows OpenAI's recent disclosure that Russian actors used ChatGPT to create a fake 'expert community' pushing talking points. It comes as U.S. AI firms sound alarms about weaponization of their own models with little public policy response from the Trump administration.
sections.whyItMatters: A frontier lab publicly documenting that its own model was used to build a full lethal-autonomy kill chain — target selection, detonation, inter-drone coordination — elevates the drone-AI proliferation debate from theory to demonstrated practice and pressures Western governments to respond.

bottomLine: Today's defense industry picture is dominated by Europe's push for independent capability — Germany opening talks with a stealth-mode U.S.-Israeli startup on a low-cost cruise missile to fill its strike gap, and Poland moving toward a sovereign 'Starlink' with ICEYE and PGZ — alongside the war-driven reshaping of American uncrewed programs, with the USAF accelerating a cheap, attritable Reaper replacement after losing roughly a quarter of its MQ-9 fleet to Iranian air defenses. The Iran war's knock-on effects keep rippling: Iran likely to reverse-engineer a captured Anduril underwater drone, a Saudi appeal for U.S. help against the Houthis answered with intelligence rather than force, and fresh reporting on Russia rehearsing subsea cable sabotage in the Arctic. The through-line is cost and autonomy: governments are buying cheaper, more expendable, locally producible systems, and hedging against dependence on U.S. infrastructure and platforms.
sources: Defense News, Defense One, Reuters, Washington Post, Anthropic report
